series.name: 2 Minutes Before
series.tagline: Nobody in this room knows they have 2 minutes left.
series.concept: The 2 minutes before a historic disaster or event. Reconstructed from survivor accounts, declassified reports, and investigative journalism. Each episode freezes time and walks through the final moments before everything changed.

episodes.title: Bhopal, December 2, 1984

slides.text: It's 11:58 PM in Bhopal. A city of 800,000 people is asleep. Inside the Union Carbide pesticide plant, the night shift is half-empty. Budget cuts meant fewer workers.
Worker Suman Dey notices Tank 610's pressure gauge is climbing. He tells his supervisor. The supervisor says, 'We'll check it after tea.' They never get to finish tea.
400 meters from the plant, the J.P. Nagar slum houses 10,000 people. A mother is breastfeeding her newborn. A rickshaw driver is counting the day's earnings. None of them know what's in Tank 610.

The tank's safety systems? All shut down. The refrigeration unit? Turned off to save money. The gas scrubber? Under maintenance. The flare tower? Disconnected. Every single safety net had a hole in it.

At midnight, Tank 610 explodes with pressure. A white cloud of poison rolls across J.P. Nagar like fog. People wake up choking, eyes burning, lungs on fire. They run — but they don't know which direction is safe. There is no safe direction.

By morning, 3,800 people were dead. Over the next weeks — 16,000 more. Half a million suffered permanent injuries. The chairman of Union Carbide never spent a single day in an Indian jail. He died in his Long Island mansion in 2014.

episodes.synopsis: Inside the Union Carbide plant, a worker notices a pressure gauge climbing. Outside, families are sleeping. In 2 minutes, 40 tons of methyl isocyanate will leak into the air.
episodes.caption: 40 tons of poison gas. Every safety system turned off. 800,000 people asleep. And one supervisor who said "after tea." What's the most chilling detail here?

episodes.title: North Atlantic, April 14, 1912

slides.text: 11:38 PM. The Titanic is cruising at nearly top speed through the North Atlantic. The night is moonless, the sea impossibly calm. Too calm. Waves would have made the iceberg easier to spot.

Lookout Frederick Fleet is in the crow's nest — 30 meters up, freezing. He's been asking for binoculars since they left port. They're locked in a cabinet. The officer with the key? Reassigned before departure. Nobody handed the key over.

Six ice warnings came in that day from other ships. Captain Smith read some and went to dinner. The last warning from SS Californian never reached the bridge — the radio operator told them to shut up, he was busy sending passenger telegrams.

Fleet sees a dark shape ahead. He stares for 30 seconds, hoping it's haze. It gets bigger. He grabs the phone to the bridge: 'Iceberg right ahead!' The officer orders hard starboard. But 46,000 tons of steel doesn't turn on a dime.

The Titanic doesn't slam into the iceberg. It scrapes along the side for 7 seconds. That gentle scrape opens 6 compartments to the sea. The ship can survive 4 flooding. Not 6. Most passengers don't even feel it.
1,517 people died that night. Not because there was no warning. Not because the iceberg was invisible. Because binoculars were locked in a cabinet. And nobody had the key.

episodes.synopsis: Lookout Frederick Fleet squints into the darkness. The binoculars are locked in a cabinet — and the officer with the key was reassigned. In 2 minutes, he'll see something that changes maritime law forever.
episodes.caption: Six warnings ignored. Binoculars locked away. A key that nobody thought to hand over. 1,517 lives — lost to a tiny oversight. Which detail shocked you most?

episodes.title: Pokhran, May 11, 1998

slides.text: 3:43 PM, Rajasthan desert. Temperature: 47°C. Underground, at the bottom of a 200-meter shaft, sits a nuclear device. Above ground, a man in a white kurta watches the sky. Not for clouds. For American satellites.

After India's 1974 test, the CIA trained satellites on Pokhran 24/7. So India's scientists worked only at night. They carried equipment dressed as villagers. They moved cables in milk trucks. By morning, the desert looked untouched.

APJ Abdul Kalam, R. Chidambaram, and a team of handpicked scientists have been preparing for 2 years. The army unit helping them was told nothing — just 'dig these shafts and don't ask questions.' Only 5 people in the entire government know the real plan.
The CIA satellite passes overhead every few minutes. Between passes, there's a gap. That gap is the window. The command is given: 'Activate.' Kalam later said his hand was steady. His heart was not.

3:45 PM. The earth shakes. A 5.0 earthquake registers on seismographs worldwide. The desert floor rises, then settles. The only thing visible from above? A faint dust cloud. The CIA didn't see it coming. Not even a little.
India became the world's sixth nuclear power. The CIA called it the biggest intelligence failure in a decade. Kalam called his mother. She said she'd seen it on TV before he could tell her.

episodes.synopsis: India's nuclear scientists are 200 meters underground. CIA satellites pass overhead every 12 minutes. APJ Abdul Kalam is watching the clock.
episodes.caption: The CIA had satellites, spies, and billions of dollars. India had milk trucks, village disguises, and scientists who worked at night. Who outplayed whom? Drop your reaction.

episodes.title: Wall Street, September 15, 2008

slides.text: 7:58 AM, Monday, September 15. New York. Lehman Brothers employees walk into their office building with coffee in hand. Some are joking. Some are nervous. None of them know that at 8 AM, their 158-year-old company will announce it's dead.

That weekend, Lehman's CEO begged every bank on Wall Street for a rescue. Bank of America said no. Barclays said maybe, then no. The government — which had bailed out Bear Stearns 6 months ago — this time said: let them fail.

Lehman had $639 billion in assets. And $619 billion in debt. That tiny gap? Mostly made of home loans given to people who couldn't pay them back. The math was broken. Everyone knew. Nobody said it out loud.
On the trading floor, screens start flashing red. A junior analyst refreshes his Bloomberg terminal. Lehman Brothers stock: $0.21. It was $86 a year ago. He doesn't move. He just stares.

8:00 AM. Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy. It's the largest bankruptcy in American history. 25,000 employees lose their jobs. Within weeks, stock markets worldwide crash. India's Sensex drops 1,000 points in a day. Your parents' savings shrink overnight.

The 2008 crash wiped out $2 trillion globally. Millions lost their homes. The bankers who caused it? Most of them got bonuses that year. One CEO left with a $480 million golden parachute. Nobody went to jail.

episodes.synopsis: Inside Lehman Brothers, employees arrive Monday morning to find security guards at the door. The bank has been dead for 48 hours — they just didn't know it yet.
episodes.caption: $639 billion empire, collapsed in a weekend. The people who broke it walked away rich. The people who trusted them lost everything. Does this make you angry? It should.

episodes.title: Chernobyl, April 26, 1986

slides.text: 1:23 AM, Pripyat, Soviet Union. Most of the 50,000 residents are asleep. At Chernobyl, the night shift is running a test on Reactor 4. The test was supposed to happen 10 hours ago, during the day shift. The experienced crew has gone home.

To run the test, they need to lower the reactor's power. They drop it too far. The reactor becomes unstable. The rulebook says: shut it down immediately. The deputy chief engineer, Dyatlov, says: continue the test. Nobody argues with Dyatlov.

Operator Leonid Toptunov is 25 years old. He sees the power readings and knows something is wrong. He hesitates. Dyatlov screams at him. Toptunov presses the button to start the test. He doesn't know it — but the reactor is now a bomb.

Power surges to 100 times the normal level in 4 seconds. Someone hits the emergency shutdown — the AZ-5 button. But the shutdown rods have a design flaw nobody was told about. Instead of stopping the reaction, they briefly accelerate it.

1:23:47 AM. Two explosions. The 1,000-ton reactor lid is blown clean off. A pillar of radioactive fire shoots into the sky. Firefighters are called. They're told it's a roof fire. They arrive in regular uniforms. No protective gear.

The explosion released 400 times more radiation than the Hiroshima bomb. 350,000 people were evacuated. Pripyat is still a ghost town today. Toptunov, the 25-year-old operator, died of radiation poisoning 3 months later in a Moscow hospital.

episodes.synopsis: Reactor 4 is running a safety test at 1:23 AM. The night shift is exhausted. The chief engineer overrides 6 safety systems.
episodes.caption: A 25-year-old operator. A boss who wouldn't listen. A design flaw nobody was told about. And an emergency button that made things worse. What haunts you most about this one?

episodes.title: Jallianwala Bagh, April 13, 1919

slides.text: 5:28 PM, Amritsar. It's Baisakhi — the harvest festival. Jallianwala Bagh is packed with families. Children playing. Farmers who came to the city for the festival. Most don't even know a curfew has been announced. There are no loudspeakers.

Brigadier General Reginald Dyer has been in Amritsar for 2 days. He's furious about protests against the Rowlatt Act. He's banned public gatherings. He marches 90 soldiers through narrow lanes toward the Bagh. With rifles. And two armored cars with machine guns.
Jallianwala Bagh has only one narrow exit. The walls are 10 feet high on every side. For a festival crowd, it's a garden. For a general with guns, it's a box with no escape.
Dyer positions his troops at the only exit. He doesn't ask the crowd to leave. He doesn't fire a warning shot. He doesn't give them a single second. He gives one order: 'Fire.'

1,650 rounds fired in 10 minutes. Soldiers were ordered to aim where the crowd was thickest. People tried to climb the walls. They jumped into the well. 120 bodies were pulled from that one well alone.

Official British count: 379 dead. Indian estimates: over 1,000. Dyer said he would have used the machine guns too, but the armored cars couldn't fit through the entrance. He was never convicted. He was called a hero in the British Parliament.

episodes.synopsis: It's Baisakhi. Thousands of families have gathered in Jallianwala Bagh. General Dyer is loading his troops. He hasn't come to talk.
episodes.caption: Families at a festival. An exit blocked by soldiers. No warning. 1,650 rounds in 10 minutes. This happened 105 years ago. The walls still have the bullet holes. What do you feel?

episodes.title: Cape Canaveral, January 28, 1986

slides.text: 11:37 AM, Cape Canaveral, Florida. It's 36°F — the coldest launch in shuttle history. In classrooms across America, children are watching on TV. Their teacher, Christa McAuliffe, is on the shuttle. She won her seat from 11,000 applicants.

The night before, engineer Roger Boisjoly called NASA and begged them to delay. The rubber O-rings sealing the rocket boosters get stiff in the cold, he said. They could crack. Leak. NASA asked his company for a formal recommendation. His managers overruled him.

7 people are strapped in. Commander Dick Scobee. Pilot Michael Smith. Christa McAuliffe, who told her students she'd teach a lesson from space. Ronald McNair, who was once refused a library card because he was Black. He read every book in that library.
11:38 AM. The countdown hits zero. The engines ignite. The shuttle lifts off perfectly. In living rooms and classrooms, people cheer. For 73 seconds, everything looks normal.

At 73 seconds, the O-ring fails. Hot gas burns through the rocket booster. The fuel tank explodes. The shuttle breaks apart at 46,000 feet. The cockpit — with the crew still conscious — falls for 2 minutes and 45 seconds before hitting the Atlantic.

Roger Boisjoly, the engineer who warned NASA, watched the launch on TV. When it exploded, he turned to his colleague and said, 'It's exactly what I told them would happen.' He spent the rest of his life haunted by it. NASA called it an 'acceptable risk.'

episodes.synopsis: Engineer Roger Boisjoly has been screaming for days that the O-rings won't hold in cold weather. NASA launches anyway. Christa McAuliffe — the first teacher in space — is on board.
episodes.caption: An engineer begged them not to launch. His bosses overruled him. 7 people died on live TV while children watched. The part that failed cost $900 and weighed less than a kilogram. What would you have done as that engineer?

episodes.title: Indian Ocean, December 26, 2004

slides.text: 7:58 AM, the coast of Tamil Nadu. Fishermen are already at sea. Families in Nagapattinam are having morning chai. On the beaches, tourists are waking up. Nobody felt the earthquake. It happened 1,600 km away, under the ocean near Sumatra.

The Pacific has a tsunami warning system. The Indian Ocean doesn't. The earthquake registered 9.1 on the Richter scale — the third largest ever recorded. Scientists in Hawaii detected it within minutes. They had no phone number to call in India.

Along the coast, the ocean suddenly pulls back. Hundreds of meters of seabed are exposed. Fish are flopping on the sand. People walk out to look. Children pick up shells. They've never seen anything like it. That's because the ocean is loading.

On a beach in Thailand, 10-year-old British tourist Tilly Smith sees the water receding. She remembers a geography lesson about tsunamis. She screams at her parents: the water pulling back means a wave is coming. Her parents clear the beach. That beach has zero deaths.

8:00 AM. A wall of water 10 meters high traveling at 800 km/h hits the coast. It doesn't crash — it just keeps coming. Inland. Through streets, hotels, temples, homes. The water doesn't stop for 15 minutes.

230,000 people died across 14 countries. In India alone — over 16,000. Entire fishing villages in Tamil Nadu were erased. The Indian Ocean got its first tsunami warning system in 2006. It took a quarter million deaths to build a phone line.

episodes.synopsis: The ocean pulls back hundreds of meters. Tourists walk out to look at the exposed seabed. They're walking toward their death.
episodes.caption: 230,000 people. Zero warning system. A 10-year-old girl saved an entire beach because of a school lesson. Meanwhile, scientists in Hawaii had the data but no one to call. What does that tell you?

episodes.title: Mumbai, November 26, 2008

slides.text: 8:58 PM, Arabian Sea, off Mumbai. A rubber dinghy cuts through dark water. 10 men on board with AK-47s, grenades, and satellite phones. They're between 21 and 28 years old. They've been training for this for a year. They've memorized Mumbai's map.

Local fishermen near Badhwar Park see the dinghy. One calls the police. 'There's a strange boat with armed men.' He's told not to panic. The call is not forwarded. The men step onto Mumbai's shore unchallenged.

On the beach, the 10 men split into 5 pairs. Each pair has a target: Taj Hotel. Oberoi Hotel. Nariman House. Leopold Cafe. CST Railway Station. They hail local taxis. The drivers have no idea what's in the bags.

9:20 PM. Two men walk into Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus. It's one of Mumbai's busiest stations — thousands of commuters heading home. They open their bags. Pull out assault rifles. And start firing into the crowd.

Mumbai burns for 60 hours. The Taj Hotel is on fire. Hostages at Nariman House. NSG commandos arrive from Delhi — but they take 10 hours because they don't have a plane on standby. 10 men hold India's financial capital hostage. 166 people die.

9 attackers were killed. 1 survived — Ajmal Kasab. He was caught at a roadblock by police with no bulletproof vests. He was hanged in 2012. The fisherman who warned the police? He never got a call back.

episodes.synopsis: Ten young men in a rubber dinghy approach Mumbai's coast. A fisherman spots them. He's ignored. The city will enter 60 hours of terror.
episodes.caption: A fisherman saw the boat. He called the police. They ignored him. 166 people died over 60 hours. One phone call could have changed everything. What would you have done differently?

episodes.title: Fukushima, March 11, 2011

slides.text: 2:44 PM, Fukushima Prefecture, Japan. The earthquake hit 50 minutes ago — 9.1 magnitude. The most powerful ever recorded in Japan. At the nuclear plant, the reactors have automatically shut down. Everything is under control. That's what they think.

Fukushima was designed to handle a 5.7-meter tsunami. In 2008, an internal study warned that a wave could reach 10 meters. The study was filed and ignored. The seawall stayed at 5.7 meters. The wave coming is 14.

The reactors are shut down, but they're still hot. They need coolant pumps running 24/7. The earthquake knocked out the power grid. No problem — they have diesel backup generators. The generators are in the basement. Below sea level.
2:46 PM. Workers at the plant see the ocean recede. Then they see the wave. 14 meters of black water, carrying ships, cars, and houses. It smashes over the 5.7-meter seawall like it isn't there.

The wave floods the basement. Every backup generator drowns. The reactors are now cooling with nothing. No power. No pumps. No water flow. The nuclear fuel rods start to heat up. And heat up. And heat up. Meltdown is now inevitable.

Three reactors melted down over the next 3 days. 154,000 people were evacuated. A 30km exclusion zone still exists today. The backup generators in the basement? That decision was made in the 1960s. Nobody moved them in 40 years.

episodes.synopsis: The Fukushima plant was built to survive a 5.7-meter tsunami. The one coming is 14 meters.
episodes.caption: A 5.7-meter wall for a 14-meter wave. Backup generators in a basement below sea level. A warning study filed and forgotten. The scariest part? Someone made all these choices. Who should answer for it?

episodes.title: Uphaar Cinema, June 13, 1997

slides.text: 5:28 PM, Green Park, New Delhi. Uphaar Cinema's balcony is packed — 800 people watching Border on its opening weekend. Families, couples, college kids. Downstairs in the basement, a Delhi Vidyut Board transformer is humming louder than usual.

The cinema has emergency exits on every floor. Most are locked or blocked. Why? The owners — the Ansal brothers — converted parts of the fire escape into a paid parking area. More revenue. Less escape. Fire extinguishers? Expired 3 years ago.

5:30 PM. The transformer in the basement explodes. Oil catches fire instantly. Thick black smoke fills the stairwells and rises through the building. The fire alarm? There isn't one. Nobody in the balcony knows yet.

The first sign: the screen flickers. Then the lights go out. Then the smoke hits. 800 people in a dark balcony, smoke filling from below. They rush to the exits. The main exits are clogged with people from lower floors. The emergency exits? Locked.

People pile onto each other at the exits. Some try to break windows — they're reinforced. Parents are holding children above the smoke. Most don't die from fire. They die from suffocation. From toxic smoke. From being crushed in the stampede.

59 dead. Over 100 injured. Most victims were in the balcony — they suffocated. The Ansal brothers were convicted 19 years later. Sentence? 2 years. One of them served the time in a hospital, not jail. The parking lot where the fire escape should have been? It's still a parking lot.

episodes.synopsis: Uphaar Cinema is screening Border. The emergency exits are chained shut. The owner converted the fire escape into extra parking.
episodes.caption: Emergency exits locked for parking revenue. No fire alarm. Expired extinguishers. 59 people suffocated in the dark. The owners got 2 years. Does that feel like justice to you?

episodes.title: Beirut, August 4, 2020

slides.text: 6:06 PM, Beirut, Lebanon. It's a regular Tuesday. Traffic. Construction. People filming TikToks on their balconies. At the port, workers are welding a broken door on Hangar 12. Inside that hangar: 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate. Enough to level a city.

The ammonium nitrate arrived on a broken cargo ship in 2013. Customs seized it. For 6 years, port officials sent letters to judges, ministers, and the military begging them to move it. Six official letters. The response? Nothing. Silence. File it.

Welding sparks land on fireworks stored in the same hangar. Yes — fireworks, next to 2,750 tons of explosive fertilizer. The fireworks catch fire. Workers call the fire brigade. The fire engine that arrives carries 1,000 liters of water. It's like spitting on a volcano.

6:07 PM. Dozens of people in Beirut see smoke at the port and start filming. The first videos show fireworks exploding in the hangar — bright flashes, loud pops. People watch from their balconies and windows. They should be running.

6:08 PM. The ammonium nitrate detonates. The explosion is equivalent to 1.1 kilotons of TNT. It produces a shockwave visible to the naked eye. It's heard in Cyprus, 240 km away. The mushroom cloud rises over a city of 2 million people.

218 dead. 7,000 injured. 300,000 people homeless. Half the city's buildings damaged. The explosion left a crater 43 meters deep. To this day, no one has been held accountable. The investigation was blocked by the politicians who ignored the letters.

episodes.synopsis: Hangar 12 has stored 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate for 6 years. Six letters begging the government to move it. All ignored. A welding team is fixing the warehouse door.
episodes.caption: 2,750 tons of explosives stored next to fireworks for 6 years. Six warning letters ignored. And the people who ignored them are now blocking the investigation into their own negligence. Does power ever face consequences?

episodes.title: Morbi, October 30, 2022

slides.text: 6:38 PM, Morbi, Gujarat. It's the day after Diwali. The Jhulto Pul — a 143-year-old British-era suspension bridge — has just reopened. Families are streaming onto it. It's a local landmark. Perfect for selfies over the Machchhu River.

The bridge was closed for 7 months for renovation. Reopened after just 5 days of actual work. The company that did it — Oreva Group — makes clocks and kitchen appliances. No structural engineers. No load testing. No safety certification.

The bridge's safe capacity was around 100 people. At 6:40 PM, there are over 500 people on it. Some are rocking it on purpose — it's a suspension bridge, it swings. Children are running in groups. The cables are carrying 5 times their rated load.

6:42 PM. A cable snaps. Then another. The bridge floor tilts. For one second, everyone is silent. Then the screaming starts. The entire middle section collapses. Hundreds of people — families, children — fall 15 meters into the river.

Most victims can't swim. It's dark. The water is cold. Parents are searching for children. Children are clinging to broken cables. Local fishermen arrive in boats before the rescue teams. They pull people out with their hands.

141 people died. 47 of them were children under 12. The Oreva Group's contract? Awarded without a tender process. Fitness certificate? Never issued. The bridge was opened on a ticket-selling basis — ₹17 per person. Revenue over safety. Again.

episodes.synopsis: A 143-year-old suspension bridge, reopened after 5 days of 'renovation' by a clock company with no engineering license. It's Diwali week. 500 people on a bridge rated for 100.
episodes.caption: A clock company 'renovated' a 143-year-old bridge. No engineers. No testing. 500 people on a bridge rated for 100. 141 dead — including 47 children. How does this keep happening?

episodes.title: Air India Flight 182, June 23, 1985

slides.text: 7:13 AM, 31,000 feet over the Atlantic Ocean. Air India's Kanishka is carrying 329 people. Families heading to India for summer vacation. 82 of the passengers are children.

The day before, a man checked a bag at Vancouver Airport for a connecting flight to Air India 182. He didn't board his connecting flight. His bag did. Airport security flagged the bag. But the X-ray operator was handling a different issue. The bag went through.

Canadian intelligence had intercepted conversations about a plot to bomb Air India. Indian intelligence had warned about Khalistani extremists targeting airlines. Both passed the information to the other. Both assumed the other would act. Neither did.

In the cargo hold, a Sanyo tuner radio packed with dynamite has a timer ticking down. The bomb was built in a Vancouver basement. It's now at 31,000 feet, surrounded by suitcases full of clothes, gifts, and sweets packed for grandparents in India.

7:14 AM. The bomb explodes at 31,000 feet. The fuselage rips open. The plane breaks apart in seconds. 329 people — including 82 children — fall into the North Atlantic. The water is 2°C. There are no survivors.

329 dead. The deadliest aviation terror attack until 9/11. The investigation took 20 years. One man was convicted. One. Canada called it the single largest mass murder in Canadian history. For years, India mourned. Canada barely remembered.

episodes.synopsis: The Kanishka is carrying 329 people. In the cargo hold, a suitcase is ticking. The passenger who checked it never boarded.
episodes.caption: Intelligence agencies on two continents knew. A bag was flagged but no one was at the screen. A passenger checked a bag and didn't board. 329 people — 82 children. The system failed at every level. What breaks your heart most?

episodes.title: Rana Plaza, April 24, 2013

slides.text: 8:43 AM, Savar, Dhaka. Rana Plaza is an 8-story building full of garment factories. 5,000 workers — mostly young women — are sewing clothes for Western brands you wear. The building was designed for 5 stories. Three more were added illegally.

Yesterday, cracks appeared in the walls and pillars. An engineer inspected and said: evacuate immediately. The shops on the ground floor closed. The garment factory owners? They told workers to come in today or lose a month's salary.

These women earn $38 a month. Losing a month's salary means their children don't eat. So they came to work. They sat at their machines. They started sewing. The building has been groaning all morning. The managers said it's normal.

8:45 AM. The power goes out — routine in Dhaka. The backup generators on the top floors kick in. The vibration from the generators travels through a building that's already cracking. It's the last straw.

8:57 AM. The building pancakes. All 8 floors collapse in 90 seconds. 5,000 people are inside. Women are buried under concrete, still clutching fabric. Some are trapped alive in air pockets. They'll stay there for days.

1,134 dead. Over 2,500 injured. Many lost limbs. The brands whose clothes they were making? Most denied any connection. One survivor was pulled out alive after 17 days. She's still sewing. She can't afford not to.

episodes.synopsis: Cracks appeared in the walls yesterday. Workers refused to enter. Owners said: come in or don't get paid. 5,000 workers are inside when the building groans.
episodes.caption: Cracks in the walls. An engineer said evacuate. Workers were told: come in or lose pay. 1,134 people died making clothes for brands you probably own. Check your closet.

episodes.title: Elphinstone Road Station, September 29, 2017

slides.text: 10:28 AM, Elphinstone Road Station, Mumbai. It's raining heavily. The narrow foot overbridge is packed — thousands squeezed shoulder to shoulder. The bridge was built for half this crowd. Welcome to Mumbai's daily gamble.

This bridge has been flagged as dangerous for years. BMC proposed a wider bridge in 2016. The file went between Railways and the city. Both said it was the other's responsibility. The file is still moving. The crowd isn't waiting.

Someone near the staircase slips on wet steps. They fall against the person ahead. A chain reaction. Someone shouts: 'The bridge is collapsing!' It's not. But in a Mumbai crowd, a rumor moves faster than truth.

Thousands try to reverse direction on a bridge 4 meters wide. People fall on the staircase. Others fall on top. In 3 minutes, bodies are piled 5 deep on the stairs. Most die from suffocation — crushed under other people.
Fellow commuters pull people out with bare hands. Local shopkeepers bring water and cloth. Ambulances take 40 minutes — streets flooded. The people of Mumbai save each other, like they always do.

23 dead. 39 injured. The bridge wasn't collapsing — it was a rumor. But the real cause? A bridge too narrow, flagged years ago, stuck in bureaucracy. The wider bridge was built 2 years later. 23 people too late.

episodes.synopsis: A narrow footbridge. 10,000+ commuters. Rain. Someone slips. Someone screams 'the bridge is collapsing.' It isn't. But the stampede is real.
episodes.caption: A bridge too narrow. A file bouncing between departments. A rumor that caused a stampede. 23 people died on a morning commute. How many bridges like this are you crossing every day?

episodes.title: Baltic Sea, September 28, 1994

slides.text: 1:13 AM, Baltic Sea. The MS Estonia is halfway between Tallinn and Stockholm. 989 passengers, most asleep. Outside, 4-meter waves. Inside, glasses sliding off tables. Normal Baltic crossing, they say.

The Estonia is a roll-on, roll-off ferry. Cars drive in through a massive bow door held by hydraulic locks. The locks have been failing for months. Crew reported it three times. Maintenance was scheduled for the next port.

1:15 AM. A massive wave hits the bow. The locks give way. The bow visor tears off — a 55-ton steel door ripped from the ship. Water floods the car deck. The crew feels the lurch. They don't know what happened.
The car deck floods in minutes. The Estonia begins listing. 15 degrees. 30. 60. Passengers wake up sliding across their cabins.
1:50 AM. The Estonia capsizes and sinks in 35 minutes. Many are trapped in cabins. Those on deck face 10°C water and 4-meter waves. Lifeboats can't launch from a listing ship.

852 dead. 137 survived. Deadliest European maritime disaster since the Titanic. A 55-ton door, three maintenance reports, and a decision to sail one more trip before fixing it. One more trip was one trip too many.

episodes.synopsis: The MS Estonia ferry. 989 passengers asleep. A bow door lock broken and reported 3 times. The sea tonight is rough.
episodes.caption: A broken lock reported 3 times. 'We'll fix it at the next port.' 852 people never made it to the next port. When was the last time something was 'scheduled for next time' in your world?

episodes.title: Balasore, June 2, 2023

slides.text: 6:53 PM, Bahanaga Bazar, Odisha. The Coromandel Express is running on time — 128 km/h. A goods train is parked on a loop line. A signaling system was recently modified. The modification was supposed to fix an old error. It created a new one.

The signal shows green — proceed. But the track points are set wrong. The train is being routed onto the loop line — directly toward the parked goods train. The driver has no way to know. The signal says go.
128 km/h. 1,200+ passengers. Families going to Chennai. Some having dinner. Some watching phone videos. The driver sees the loop line ahead. By the time he realizes, there's no distance to brake.

6:55 PM. The Coromandel slams into the goods train at full speed. Coaches derail and fly onto the adjacent line. The Bengaluru-Howrah Express is on that line. Traveling opposite direction. It hits the derailed coaches.
Three trains. Coaches stacked like crushed tin cans. Locals arrive before rescue teams. They use phone flashlights to search wreckage. They pull survivors out with their hands.

296 dead. Over 1,200 injured. India's deadliest train crash in decades. The cause: a signaling error during maintenance that was never tested. A fix that created the disaster it was supposed to prevent.

episodes.synopsis: Three trains converge near Bahanaga Bazar. A signaling modification hasn't been tested. The Coromandel Express is on the wrong track at 128 km/h.
episodes.caption: Three trains. One signal. A maintenance fix never tested. 296 people died on a routine journey. India's railways carry 23 million daily. How safe do you feel?

episodes.title: MV Sewol, April 16, 2014

slides.text: 8:48 AM, off South Korea's coast. The MV Sewol carries 476 people to Jeju Island. 325 are students on a class trip. They're filming selfie videos. The ship begins to tilt.
The PA crackles: 'Stay where you are. Remain in your cabins.' The students listen. They text parents: 'The ship is tilting. They told us to stay.' They've been taught to obey authority.

While students obey, Captain Lee Joon-seok doesn't issue an evacuation. The coast guard calls — he says he's 'assessing.' Then he walks to the deck. Boards a rescue boat. In his underwear. He's one of the first to leave.
Ship tilts past 45 degrees. Cabins flood. Students who stayed are trapped. Some send final texts: 'I love you, Mom.' 'I don't think I'm going to make it.' The PA never said evacuate.

The Sewol capsizes. 172 students escape — mostly those who ignored the announcement and jumped. The 153 who obeyed? Drowned in their cabins. Divers found them grouped together. Still in their spots. Still wearing life jackets.
304 dead. 250 were high school students. The captain survived — sentenced to 36 years. He told kids to stay while he ran. The ones who survived disobeyed. The ones who listened are gone.

episodes.synopsis: A ferry sinking. 325 high school students told to stay in cabins. The captain escapes first. The students who obeyed drowned. Those who disobeyed survived.
episodes.caption: The captain told students to stay. He escaped first. Students who obeyed died. Students who disobeyed survived. What does blind obedience to authority cost?

episodes.title: Vizag Gas Leak, May 7, 2020

slides.text: 2:58 AM, Visakhapatnam. COVID lockdown. The LG Polymers plant is restarting after 40 days. Styrene must be kept cold. No one monitored the temperature during lockdown.
Styrene must stay below 20°C. Above that, it self-polymerizes — a runaway reaction. The tank temperature? Nobody checked. It had been climbing for weeks.
RR Venkatapuram is 500 meters away. 3,000 families asleep. Lockdown means empty streets. A white gas creeps through the village.
People wake choking. Eyes burning. Children vomiting. They stumble into the gas cloud. Can't see. Can't breathe. Some collapse. Others run blind.
Hospitals are COVID-only. Gas victims turned away. People collapse in parking lots. The gas dissipates by dawn. The damage is done.
12 dead. Thousands hospitalized. The plant operated on expired clearance. Same country. Same negligence. Bhopal — 36 years earlier. Different chemical. Same story.

episodes.synopsis: COVID lockdown. LG Polymers plant shut 40 days. Restarting with no safety checks. Styrene tanks overheating for weeks. A neighborhood 500 meters away.
episodes.caption: Plant shut 40 days. No monitoring. Tanks overheating. Homes 500 meters away. Hospitals locked for COVID. 36 years after Bhopal, same story. Will we ever learn?

episodes.title: Grenfell Tower, June 14, 2017

slides.text: 12:52 AM, North Kensington, London. Grenfell Tower houses 600 people. Recently renovated with new cladding — to look modern. The cladding cost £2 less per panel than the fireproof option.
4th floor fridge catches fire. Firefighters arrive in 6 minutes. Kitchen fire put out. But it's reached the window. Outside the window — the cladding.

The cladding is polyethylene — plastic — between thin aluminum. Chosen over fire-resistant option to save £5,000 on a £10 million renovation. Fire races up the building like a lit match on a matchbox.

Residents call 999. Told to stay in their flats — standard advice for concrete towers. But this fire is on the outside of every floor simultaneously. By the time 'stay put' is reversed, some floors are unreachable.
By 1:30 AM, the entire tower is engulfed. People wave flashlights from windows. Some jump. A mother drops her baby from the 10th floor. The baby survives.

72 dead. Residents had warned about fire safety for years. Ignored. The cladding was banned in Germany and the US. £5,000 saved — that's £69 per life. Hundreds of UK buildings still have the same cladding.

episodes.synopsis: A fridge catches fire on the 4th floor. The building's decorative cladding — installed to look prettier for rich neighbors — is essentially fuel. 72 dead.
episodes.caption: A fridge fire. £5,000 saved on cladding. 'Stay put' advice that killed people. Residents warned for years — ignored because they were poor. 72 lives. How much is a life worth?

episodes.title: Kedarnath, June 16, 2013

slides.text: 6:58 PM, Kedarnath. 3 days of nonstop rain. Thousands stranded. Above the temple, Chorabari Tal is about to overflow.
Scientists warned Chorabari Tal was dangerous. The report went to the state government. They were busy — peak pilgrimage season. Maximum revenue.
7:00 PM. Chorabari Tal bursts. Not just water — boulders, mud, trees. By the time it reaches Kedarnath: a 40-foot wall moving at 70 km/h.
The flood hits Kedarnath. Everything flattened. The 1,200-year-old temple survives — a massive boulder lodges behind it, splitting the flood. The temple stands. Everything around it is gone.
The flood doesn't stop. Town after town wiped out. 100,000 pilgrims stranded. No roads. No food. No communication.
Official toll: 5,748. Estimates: 10,000+. Thousands still missing. IAF ran the largest civilian rescue in history. The lake scientists warned about? It emptied itself on Kedarnath.

episodes.synopsis: Thousands of pilgrims at Kedarnath. Rain for 3 days. Chorabari Tal at max capacity. Scientists warned. Nobody evacuated.
episodes.caption: Scientists warned about the lake. Government was focused on pilgrimage revenue. 10,000+ dead or missing. The temple survived. The people didn't. Nature warned us. We didn't listen.

episodes.title: Hiroshima, August 6, 1945

slides.text: 8:13 AM, Hiroshima, Japan. Monday morning. Streetcars running. Children walking to school. 350,000 people. Above — invisible at 31,000 feet — the Enola Gay has opened its bomb bay doors.
Pilot Tibbets named the plane after his mother. The bomb weighs 4,400 kg. The crew was told it's powerful. Nobody told them it would vaporize a city.
8:15 AM. Little Boy falls. 44.4 seconds to reach detonation altitude. On the ground, people look up and see a parachute — the measurement instruments. They don't see the bomb.

A flash brighter than the sun. 4,000°C at ground zero. People within 1 km vaporized — they leave shadows burned into concrete. A woman's shadow etched onto bank steps. She was sitting there, waiting for it to open.
80,000 die instantly. By year's end: 140,000. Sadako Sasaki, 1.7 km from ground zero, survives. Develops leukemia at 12. She tries to fold 1,000 paper cranes. Makes 644.
Sadako's statue stands in Hiroshima's Peace Park. Children worldwide send paper cranes. The pile never shrinks. People keep sending them.

episodes.synopsis: 31,000 feet above Hiroshima. The crew has a bomb they don't understand. Below, 350,000 people are starting Monday morning.
episodes.caption: 44.4 seconds of falling. 80,000 in an instant. A girl who folded 644 cranes hoping to live. Which moment will you carry with you?

episodes.title: The Kursk Submarine, August 12, 2000

slides.text: 11:26 AM, Barents Sea. The nuclear submarine Kursk is 80 meters below. 118 crew. A practice torpedo is leaking hydrogen peroxide fuel. Nobody notices.
11:28 AM. Small explosion in the torpedo room — 2.2 on the Richter scale. 11:30 AM. Second explosion — 250 times more powerful. Rips open the bow. Kursk slams into the sea floor at 107 meters.

23 sailors in the rear compartment survive. They seal the bulkhead. No power. In the dark, they write letters. Captain Kolesnikov writes: 'It's dark here. But I'll try not to despair. Regards to everyone. Don't worry.'

Russia knows within hours. Putin stays on vacation. Russia refuses help from Norway and Britain for 5 days. Their own rescue subs can't dock — too old. Norway opens the hatch in hours. Day 9. Everyone is dead.
The 23 had about 6 hours of air. If help came in time, they'd have lived. Kolesnikov's letter was found in his pocket. His wife received it months later.
118 dead. 23 survived the explosion. They had air for 6 hours. Russia waited 5 days. Those men wrote goodbye letters in the dark — waiting for rescue that never came.

episodes.synopsis: 118 men. A torpedo leaking fuel. Two explosions. 23 survivors write goodbye letters in the dark. Russia refuses help for 5 days.
episodes.caption: 23 men survived the explosion. 6 hours of air. Russia waited 5 days to accept help. They wrote goodbye letters in the dark. What kind of system lets that happen?

episodes.title: Right Now

slides.text: You've seen 24 episodes. 24 disasters. Every single one had a warning. A report filed. A phone call made. A scientist who said 'this will happen.' Not one came without a signal.
Right now, climate scientists are filing reports. Engineers flagging bridges. Doctors warning about antibiotic resistance. The reports are being filed.

The pattern: Step 1 — Warning given. Step 2 — It costs money to fix. Step 3 — Someone decides the risk is 'acceptable.' Step 4 — Time runs out. Step 5 — 'How did this happen?' It happened at Step 3. Every time.
Which 2 minutes are we in right now? Before a dam breaks? Before a building collapses? You are always in someone's '2 minutes before.'
Every disaster was preventable. Not with technology. With a phone call returned. A report read. A lock fixed. A generator moved. Small, boring actions nobody did.

Nobody in this room knows they have 2 minutes left. That's how every story began. The question isn't whether there's a countdown somewhere. There is. The question is: when the warning comes to your desk — what will you do with it?

episodes.synopsis: The final episode turns the lens on the present. Every disaster had a warning. What's being ignored right now?
episodes.caption: 24 disasters. 24 warnings. 24 times someone decided the risk was 'acceptable.' This isn't history. This is now. What report is gathering dust that has YOUR name in the consequences? Stay awake.
